name: Harlingen
title: Ship Thickness Measurement in Harlingen | Coasters & Ferries
description: Ship thickness measurement in Harlingen for coasters, island ferries and workboats: hold, hatch cover and shell UTM, plus gauging at the shiplift yard.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Gauging for Coasters, Ferries and Workboats in Harlingen
intro: Harlingen is Friesland's seaport, reached from the North Sea through the tidal channels of the Wadden Sea. Coasters bring in and carry away bulk and general cargo, Doeksen's ferries run to Terschelling and Vlieland, and fishing boats, traditional sailing ships and workboats fill the inner harbours. Damen Shiprepair Harlingen lifts vessels out on its shiplift and repairs them under cover, so many small ships come here for docking and survey. Atlantis sends technicians from India to each vessel, whether it sits on the repair platform or at a cargo quay.

highlights.p: Damen Shiprepair Harlingen raises vessels on a shiplift onto a repair platform, with covered halls for blasting, painting and repair. A ship can stay dry and sheltered for days, which suits a complete renewal survey gauging of bottom, double bottom and holds whatever the weather.

Short-sea general cargo ships load and discharge at Harlingen's quays within a day or two. Hold plating, tank tops, hatch covers and coamings can be gauged as soon as a hold is empty and swept, while cargo work carries on in the other holds.

highlights.h: Island ferries outside the busy season
highlights.p: Ferries to Terschelling and Vlieland run their fullest timetable in summer. Shell plating, car decks, ramps, voids and steering gear flats are gauged when a vessel is rotated out of service, often in combination with a docking at the yard across the harbour.

port.h: Harlingen and its Wadden Sea approach
p: Harlingen lies on the Frisian shore of the Wadden Sea, inside the gap between Vlieland and Terschelling through which ships reach it from the North Sea. The approach follows dredged channels across tidal flats, and the depth available rises and falls with the tide, so masters of loaded coasters plan arrival and departure around high water and the port's controlling depths. The Wadden Sea is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and an IMO Particularly Sensitive Sea Area, which brings careful routeing rules and close attention to anything that could pollute its waters. Behind the town, the Van Harinxma Canal carries inland vessels towards Leeuwarden and the Frisian waterways, so Harlingen also works as a transfer point between sea-going ships and barges.

Cargo here is short-sea and regional. Coasters carry salt, sand and aggregates, agricultural bulk, fertiliser, timber and project items to and from ports around the North Sea, the Baltic and the British Isles, and some of that cargo continues inland by barge. The ferry harbour is busy all year with Doeksen's services to Terschelling and Vlieland, which combine conventional car ferries with fast passenger craft. A fishing fleet works from the port, and the inner harbours are a home base for the traditional sailing ships of the Dutch brown fleet, many of them former cargo vessels that now take passengers out on the Wadden Sea and the IJsselmeer. Dredgers, survey craft, tugs and offshore workboats complete the harbour's regular traffic.

Ship repair is as much a part of Harlingen as cargo. The yard on the harbour front traces its history back to 1600 and now operates as Damen Shiprepair Harlingen, with a shiplift, a large repair platform, covered blasting and repair halls and a row of repair berths. It takes vessels of up to about 130 metres, including tankers presented gas-free or inerted, so coasters, ferries, workboats and other small and mid-sized ships arrive from well beyond Friesland for their dockings. Thickness gauging in Harlingen is therefore often part of a full docking programme rather than a quick check during a cargo call, and owners can have steel renewed under cover straight after the readings are taken, without waiting for dry weather.

facilities.h: Shiplift, repair platform and cargo quays in Harlingen
p: Dockings at Harlingen use the shiplift rather than a floating or graving dock. The vessel is raised onto the repair platform or moved into a covered hall, where the bottom, sides, rudder, sea chests and propeller area stay exposed for as long as the work needs. For thickness gauging that is close to ideal: the yard provides staging and lighting, the halls keep surfaces dry for couplant and marking, and the class surveyor can follow the close-up programme at the same time. Plates found with substantial or excessive corrosion can be marked directly on the steel for the yard's renewal crew.

Gauging afloat takes place at the cargo quays, the ferry harbour and the yard's repair berths. Coasters can be measured hold by hold while cargo work continues elsewhere on board, and ballast tanks can be added if the crew can empty and ventilate them within the call. Ferries are best gauged when the operator rotates a vessel out of the timetable. Ships with afloat repairs but no docking due often lie at the yard's berths, and those periods suit piping, deck and tank gauging that defines what has to be replaced. Deep-draught ships cannot reach Harlingen, so the yard's work and the port's traffic both centre on small and mid-sized vessels.
list: Damen Shiprepair Harlingen shiplift and repair platform — renewal and docking survey gauging of shell, double bottom, sea chests and holds with the ship dry.
Covered blasting and repair halls — hull, tank and internal structure readings taken under cover, unaffected by wind or rain.
The yard's repair berths — afloat gauging of piping, decks and tanks during repair periods that do not need a docking.
Cargo quays in the commercial harbour — hold, tank-top, hatch cover and coaming readings on coasters between discharge and loading.
Ferry harbour — deck, ramp, void and shell readings on the Terschelling and Vlieland ferries when they are taken out of the timetable.
Inner and fishing harbours — hull and deck readings on fishing vessels and traditional sailing ships lying alongside.

context.h: Protected waters, island links and the rules behind Harlingen gauging
p: Port state control in Harlingen is carried out by the Human Environment and Transport Inspectorate (ILT) within the Paris MoU, and foreign-flagged coasters calling here are inspected under the same regime as any ship in a Dutch port. Coasters tend to be older than the deep-sea fleet, built with box-shaped holds and pontoon or folding hatch covers, and an inspector boarding an elderly general cargo ship looks hard at the hatch covers, coamings and air pipes for wastage and holes. Gauging those items before arrival, rather than after a deficiency has been written, is one of the commonest requests from the managers of small cargo ships.

The island ferries bring their own pressures. They are domestic passenger ships that berth and unberth many times a day in all weathers, so shell plating, fendering, ramps and their hinges take repeated loads, and operators keep to tight maintenance schedules to avoid losing sailings. Because every ship approaching Harlingen crosses a protected sea, the authorities treat a leaking hull, a failed overboard line or a fuel spill in the Wadden Sea with particular seriousness. For managers of older coasters, that is one more reason to know the condition of the double bottom, the side shell and the fuel and ballast tanks before the ship is brought in on the tide.

jobs.p: Harlingen jobs divide between full dockings at the shiplift yard and shorter work on ships at the cargo and ferry quays. A docking gives time for a complete renewal survey programme, with the yard ready to renew steel as soon as readings are reported. A cargo call gives a day or two for targeted gauging of holds and hatch covers, and ferry work follows the operator's rotation. On older coasters, owners increasingly ask for a condition gauging before deciding whether the next renewal survey is worth doing at all, and that decision often rests on the state of the hatch covers and the double bottom. Examples of the jobs we plan here:
list: A coaster on the shiplift for its third renewal survey: double bottom, tank top, side shell and transverse bulkheads gauged to the TM plan, with substantial corrosion marked for renewal.
A general cargo ship discharging at the commercial quays: hatch cover plating, coaming top plates and air pipes gauged ahead of an expected port state control inspection.
An island car ferry rotated out of the timetable: car-deck plating, ramp structure, voids and side shell gauged before its docking at the local yard.
A traditional sailing ship carrying passengers: shell plating and frames gauged and seams examined ahead of its periodic survey.
A dredger or workboat in an afloat repair period at the yard's berths: hopper, pipework and tank readings that define the repair list.

logistics: The team normally lands at Amsterdam Schiphol and continues north by train or road; trains run to Harlingen by way of Leeuwarden, and Groningen Airport Eelde offers some European connections. The shipyard and the cargo quays have controlled access, so the ship's agent or the yard registers the technicians before they arrive. Our technicians travel from India on Schengen visas that must be applied for well ahead of the job; for a docking at the Harlingen yard the slot is usually fixed early enough to make that straightforward.
vessels: Coasters and short-sea general cargo ships

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in Harlingen, or only a shiplift?
faqs.a: Harlingen's docking facility is the shiplift at Damen Shiprepair Harlingen, which raises vessels onto a repair platform with covered halls beside it. For gauging the effect is the same as a drydock: the hull is dry and accessible, and the yard supplies staging and lighting. Ships too large for the shiplift dock at yards elsewhere in the Netherlands or Germany, and can be gauged in Harlingen beforehand.

faqs.q: Can hatch covers be gauged while a coaster is loading in Harlingen?
faqs.a: Yes, on the covers over holds that are not being worked, and on the rest as soon as loading allows. Pontoon covers can be gauged on the quay if the stevedores land them there, while folding covers are measured in place. Coaming top plates and drain channels are checked in the same visit, because together with the covers they decide whether the holds stay weathertight.

faqs.q: Does the tide limit when a ship can reach Harlingen for a job?
faqs.a: It can. Loaded coasters often need high water to cross the channels of the Wadden Sea, so their arrival follows the tide and may shift by several hours. We base the team's boarding time on the agent's latest berthing estimate and adjust as it changes. Once the ship is alongside or on the shiplift, the tide no longer affects the gauging.

faqs.q: Can you gauge the old steel hulls of traditional sailing ships?
faqs.a: Yes. Old hull plating can be measured with ultrasonic gauges once paint and scale are removed at each point, and readings next to rivets and seams show where plates have thinned. Heavily pitted plating needs care, because single readings can miss the deepest pits, so we take closer patterns where the surface calls for it and report pitting depths separately from general wastage.

faqs.q: Can steel renewal start at Harlingen as soon as readings are reported?
faqs.a: That is how many dockings here run. We report substantial and excessive corrosion to the superintendent and the attending surveyor every day, mark the affected plates, and the yard can prepare renewal while gauging continues elsewhere on the ship. The final report on the class formats then records the readings and identifies the areas that were renewed.
